---
title: "Random-effect correlations"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

The [random-slope page](random-slopes.qmd) gave each MALD participant a baseline deviation and a lexical-frequency-slope deviation. The two deviations may themselves be related across the participant population. The [centering page](centering-predictors.qmd) reminds us that an intercept is the fitted value at a chosen predictor zero, so an intercept-slope correlation inherits that choice.

Recall that [correlation](../random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd) standardizes covariance by two standard deviations; [variance, covariance, and standard deviation](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) refer here to participant-level latent deviations. Conditional [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) concerns trial responses after those deviations are supplied. The resulting correlation describes response patterns across repeated MALD trials, not a correlation among lexical properties.

We first write the joint deviation distribution, then fit its covariance on centered predictors and show why changing the intercept reference changes the correlation parameter.

## Writing one joint distribution

For participant $p$, model

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
b_{0p}\\
b_{1p}
\end{pmatrix}
\sim
\mathcal N
\left(
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}
\tau_0^2 & \rho\tau_0\tau_1\\
\rho\tau_0\tau_1 & \tau_1^2
\end{pmatrix}
\right).
$$

The parameter $\rho$ is the correlation between participant intercept and frequency-slope deviations. A positive value means that participants above the population baseline tend to have frequency slopes above the population slope. The sign of *above* depends on the response and predictor coding.

If $\rho=0$, the model treats the deviations as uncorrelated. It does not set either variance to zero; participants may still vary substantially in both dimensions.

## Fitting the covariance on centered predictors

```{r}
#| label: mald-random-correlation
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
mald <- subset(mald, correct == 1L)

standardize <- function(x) {
  as.numeric(scale(x))
}

mald$z_frequency <- standardize(mald$log_frequency_subtlex)
mald$z_duration <- standardize(mald$log_duration)
mald$z_trial <- standardize(mald$trial_order)

fit <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ z_frequency + z_duration + z_trial +
    (1 + z_frequency | participant_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mald,
  control = lmerControl(
    optimizer = "bobyqa",
    optCtrl = list(maxfun = 200000L)
  )
)

participant_covariance <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit))
participant_correlation <- participant_covariance$sdcor[
  participant_covariance$grp == "participant_id" &
    participant_covariance$var1 == "(Intercept)" &
    !is.na(participant_covariance$var2) &
    participant_covariance$var2 == "z_frequency"
]
frequency_slope_sd <- participant_covariance$sdcor[
  participant_covariance$grp == "participant_id" &
    participant_covariance$var1 == "z_frequency" &
    is.na(participant_covariance$var2)
]

c(
  intercept_frequency_correlation = participant_correlation,
  frequency_slope_sd = frequency_slope_sd
)
```

The fitted correlation is `r sprintf("%.3f", participant_correlation)`. Its meaning is tied to the intercept at mean log frequency, mean log duration, and mean trial order. The fitted slope standard deviation is only `r sprintf("%.4f", frequency_slope_sd)` log-response-time units, so a strong substantive story about the correlation would outrun the estimated slope variation.

## Why centering changes the correlation

Let the centered predictor be

$$
x_i^{c}=x_i-c.
$$

Because $x_i=x_i^c+c$, the group-specific part becomes

$$
b_{0p}+b_{1p}x_i
=(b_{0p}+cb_{1p})+b_{1p}x_i^c.
$$

The new intercept deviation is thus

$$
b'_{0p}=b_{0p}+cb_{1p}.
$$

Its covariance with the unchanged slope is

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(b'_{0p},b_{1p})
=\operatorname{Cov}(b_{0p},b_{1p})
+c\operatorname{Var}[b_{1p}].
$$

Centering changes the point on each fitted line called the intercept. It can thus change the intercept-slope correlation without changing any fitted line or response.

For two centering constants $c_1$ and $c_2$, the same fitted group lines are represented by intercept deviations $b_{0p}+c_1b_{1p}$ and $b_{0p}+c_2b_{1p}$. Their correlations with $b_{1p}$ generally differ because the covariance changes by $c\operatorname{Var}[b_{1p}]$. Thus $\rho$ is a parameter of a coded covariance structure, not a correlation between two independently observed listener traits.

In `lmer`, `(1 + z_frequency | participant_id)` estimates the intercept-slope covariance. `(1 + z_frequency || participant_id)` sets that covariance to zero while retaining both variance components. The second form is a substantive independence restriction; it is not merely a faster spelling of the first.

```{r}
#| label: random-correlation-plot
participant_effects <- ranef(fit)$participant_id
effect_plot <- data.frame(
  intercept_deviation = participant_effects[["(Intercept)"]],
  slope_deviation = participant_effects[["z_frequency"]]
)

ggplot(
  effect_plot,
  aes(x = intercept_deviation, y = slope_deviation)
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey80", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey80", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, color = "#1F5A85") +
  labs(
    x = "Intercept conditional mode at mean predictors",
    y = "Frequency-slope conditional mode"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The points are conditional modes, not independently observed participant traits, and their empirical scatter is not a replacement for $\widehat\rho$ from the covariance model. The display makes the fitted group dimensions visible while the model accounts for shrinkage and conditional uncertainty.

A correlation near an endpoint can reflect a stable population relation or weak information in an over-rich covariance structure. It should be interpreted with the two standard deviations, the number of participant levels, and the singularity diagnostic.

## Recap and check

1. Is the empirical correlation of `ranef()` points equal to $\widehat\rho$? No. Conditional modes are shrunken and have unequal uncertainty; `VarCorr()` reports the covariance-model estimate.
2. Does `||` remove the random slope? No. It retains intercept and slope variation while constraining their covariance to zero.

The [next page](singular-fits.qmd) develops the rank diagnostic directly.
